understanding, from reading the source, of what is happening\r\n\r\nThe runtime itself does not send telemetry so you shouldn't be sending any in telemetry production regardless of the environment setting by using the runtime package and running your pre-built app with the shared runtime by doing:\r\n\r\n`dotnet my.dll`\r\n\r\nThis is also confirmed as the [intention from the documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/telemetry)\r\n\r\n\u003e Telemetry isn't enabled when using the dotnet command itself, with no command attached:\r\n\u003e * dotnet\r\n\u003e * dotnet [path-to-app]\r\n\r\nEqually a `self-contained deployment` will produce an executable file that requires nothing to be installed on the target machine and will not send any telemetry when running that executable.\r\n\r\nThe sdk *does* send telemetry; this is also confirmed as the [intention from the documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/telemetry)\r\n\r\n\u003e Telemetry is enabled when using the .NET Core CLI commands, such as:\r\n\u003e * dotnet build\r\n\u003e * dotnet pack\r\n\u003e * dotnet restore\r\n\u003e * dotnet run\r\n\r\nThe first install/run at command line  that prints the message about `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT` uses the `FirstTimeUseNoticeSentinel` which does ***not*** send any telemetry if it *also* is printing the message; so you are warned prior to it sending telemetry.\r\n\r\nIt does not send any telemetry after that if the `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT` set to one of `true`, `1`, `yes` (case insensitive)\r\n\r\nThe HIPAA example @sushihangover gave compiles programs in production so it is using the full *sdk* rather than just the *runtime*.\r\n\r\nThe workarounds to the telemetry when using the sdk (`build`/`run` etc) as I understand them are:\r\n\r\n* either, set `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT` environment variable\r\n* or, use `MsBuild` rather than `dotnet` to build your app - its what `dotnet` ends up calling and it doesn't send telemetry - its also less convenient; but what you'd probably be using on your build server\r\n\r\nNot sure what the Windows desktop installer does first time; there is a `IsDotnetBeingInvokedFromNativeInstaller` path which does something different\r\n\r\n**tl;dr**\r\n\r\nIf you receive the message\r\n\r\n\u003e Welcome to .NET Core!\r\n\u003e `---------------------\r\n\u003e Learn more about .NET Core: https://aka.ms/dotnet-docs\r\n\u003e Use 'dotnet --help' to see available commands or visit: https://aka.ms/dotnet-cli-docs\r\n\u003e\r\n\u003e Telemetry\r\n\u003e `---------\r\n\u003e The .NET Core tools collect usage data in order to help us improve your experience. You can opt-out of telemetry by setting the DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT environment variable to '1' or 'true' using your favorite shell.\r\n\u003e\r\n\u003e Read more about .NET Core CLI Tools telemetry: https://aka.ms/dotnet-cli-telemetry\r\n\r\n**That use will not report any telemetry**; dir="auto">I thought to better frame this discussion it might be worth while to explore <em>what</em> telemetry is collected. I did my best to capture this, and have probably gotten some of this wrong.</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto">The <em>name</em> of the command that is run, like <code class="notranslate">dotnet *foo*</code>. <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/blob/58c580dbcc212846d38820d015e73f2d7e80214e/src/dotnet/Program.cs#L148">https://github.com/dotnet/cli/blob/58c580dbcc212846d38820d015e73f2d7e80214e/src/dotnet/Program.cs#L148</a>. It does not appear to collect the arguments passed to the command.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">When installation is complete successfully. It appears to also collect the name of the exe files that did the installation. <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/blob/5a37290f24aba5d35f3f958300aa20329e5ccaa7/src/dotnet/commands/dotnet-internal-reportinstallsuccess/InternalReportinstallsuccessCommand.cs#L33">https://github.com/dotnet/cli/blob/5a37290f24aba5d35f3f958300aa20329e5ccaa7/src/dotnet/commands/dotnet-internal-reportinstallsuccess/InternalReportinstallsuccessCommand.cs#L33</a></p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">Any telemetry logged by MSbuild. This is done by creating a <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/blob/3471d437969ed52d12116f7067b02e6e12a49d03/src/dotnet/commands/dotnet-msbuild/MSBuildLogger.cs">logger</a> and handling only telemetry events from MSBuild. This is a rather complicated subject in MSBuild and wasn't very easy for me to follow, so if there are concerns of interest in MSBuild telemetry, perhaps the issue is best raised there.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">Detailed information about <code class="notranslate">dotnet new</code>. However, none of this appears to contain personal information. It is mostly the template and language that is used in <code class="notranslate">dotnet new</code>, or if you used the help parameter.  <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/rel/vs2017/3-Preview3/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Cli/New3Command.cs#L916">https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/rel/vs2017/3-Preview3/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Cli/New3Command.cs#L916</a></p>
</li>
</ol></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li It should be OPTIN.</p>
<p dir="auto">Rationale for this being a bad idea:</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>This defines the set of data currently collected. If this changes, it may collect more data. That means to ensure that it doesn't leak data, you have to audit every release to ensure telemetry hasn't changed.</li>
<li>There's no test case.</li>
<li>It, as most MSFT products these days, shows absolutely no respect for the end user's preferences.</li>
<li>EU Article 29 Working Party are still miffed about the opt-out Windows 10 telemetry. Adding it to your development tool chain is just throwing gas on the fire.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">There's enough case to change this to opt in. This is met with silence which is unacceptable. It's like the MS Connect issue I opened against IE9 after they broke ClickOnce when the new download bar turned up. Suck it up and accept it and when you provide evidence, silence.</p>
<p dir="auto">Go doesn't call home.</p>
<p dir="auto">Python doesn't call home.</p>
<p dir="auto">Vim doesn't call home.</p>

<h3 dir="auto"><a href="https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/dotnet/2017/07/21/what-weve-learned-from-net-core-sdk-telemetry/" rel="nofollow">What we’ve learned from .NET Core SDK Telemetry</a></h3>
<p dir="auto">We are releasing .NET Core SDK usage data that has been collected by the .NET Core CLI. We have been using this data to determine the most common CLI scenarios, the distribution of operating systems and to answer other questions we’ve had, as described below.</p>
<p dir="auto">As an open source application platform that collects usage data via an SDK, it is important that all developers that work on the project have access to usage data in order to fully participate in and understand design choices and propose product changes. This is now the case with .NET Core.</p>
<p dir="auto">.NET Core telemetry was first announced in the .NET Core 1.0 RC2 and .NET Core 1.0 RTW blog announcements. It is also documented in .NET Core telemetry docs.</p>
<p dir="auto">We will release new data on a quarterly schedule going forward. The data is licensed with the Open Data Commons Attribution License.</p>

<p dir="auto">This is indicated by the fact that every time telemetry is mentioned with any product that MSFT ships a very slightly different question is being answered. Same with windows 10 telemetry where the silence is deafening. Is it the party line inside MSFT to not answer the same questions and drown them out with marketing and blog posts?</p>
<p dir="auto">On top of this it's quite difficult getting this past security controls in some corporates. If your product calls home by default you're off then tender list immediately. There is not even any discussion on the matter.</p>
<p dir="auto">Transparency is not showing us what you collect, it is explicitly asking to collect it. <p dir="auto">I would be happy to entertain more opt-out options along the lines of <a href="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/issues/6086">https://github.com/dotnet/cli/issues/6086</a>. I'm going to focus on that. The current model of telemetry is very useful given the usefulness of the data that it produces (as discussed in the blog post). It is very important for our future development that we continue to have access to the data.</p>
<p dir="auto">I'm closing this issue. We've heard that feedback and are choosing to continue with the same model. I know that's a disappointment to the folks on the thread (and others). <p dir="auto"><a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/richlander/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/richlander">@richlander</a>: I'm closing this issue. We've heard that feedback and are choosing to continue with the same model.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">I would like to point out, that, without informed, prior consent, collecting <strong>any</strong> personal information is illegal in most jurisdictions. There is sufficient precedent in the EU data protection directives 1995/46/EC, now superseded by <a href="http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32016R0679" rel="nofollow">2016/679/EC</a>, as well as similar legislation in the state of New York (not sure which one at the moment) that collection of any data amounts to collection of personally identifiable information, as the time the data is collected and the information about where on the internet it is sent from can often, though sometimes inaccurately, identify a person, and is often treated as such information.<br>
The only way you can comply with the legislation is to ensure every user of your software is prompted and asked for consent (which you cannot reliably do, as computers may be in shared use in a manner that should be obvious to you) or to make telemetry collection an opt-in setting as specified in pulls <a class="issue-link js-issue-link" data-error-text="Failed to load title" data-id="241282746" data-permission-text="Title is private" data-url="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/issues/7096" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/dotnet/cli/pull/7096/hovercard" href="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/pull/7096">dotnet/cli#7096</a> and <a class="issue-link js-issue-link" data-error-text="Failed to load title" data-id="241300361" data-permission-text="Title is private" data-url="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/issues/7098" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/dotnet/cli/pull/7098/hovercard" href="https://github.com/dotnet/cli/pull/7098">dotnet/cli#7098</a> .<br>
Yes, I understand this means you will most likely not get any or poor telemetry results. You are going to have to live with that, or stop distributing your software in the aforementioned markets. Blocking telemetry requests on a geoIP basis on your servers does not meet the requirement.<br>
Feel free to contact the legal department. href="https://github.com/jankun">@jankun</a><br>
I know this issue is closed but it's quite an interesting topic so just wanted to leave some feedback.<br>
I agree that there should be a checkbox on the installer.<br>
The only reason not to have a checkbox on the installer (or any other kind of Yes/no experience), is because <strong><em>it makes it too easy</em></strong> for users to express a desire to opt out. <strong>You want to make this difficult</strong>, right?. Even if its a small step to go and set an environment variable - 'it's still a step!'. This will mean you still get the data for the portion of people who are too lazy or simply forget to follow up and set that environment variable. That's <em>more data for you</em>.</p>
<p dir="auto">Also we are trained these days to bypass lots of boring text, and look for the things that we need to engage with on forms. When running through an installer - does anyone actually read the end user licence agreement in it's entirety? Ofcourse not! We have been trained to scan for the UI elements that actually require engagement of some kind. So:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>A bit of text explaining some stuff about telemetry - meh - not important - you can't change this text or have any impact on it right now.</li>
<li>A checkbox confirming whether I want telemetry enabled? Ok thats actually engaging me with a question. I'll respond.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Microsoft don't want to truly engage you with this question - they need this data. This data makes the product better. That means <em>they don't really want you to have a choice</em>.</p>
<p dir="auto">It's a shame because when users are given a choice, and they do <strong>choose</strong> to help improve a product - you garner loyalty from that user at the same time. The user, feels like they chose to help the product and this in turn makes them feel valued - <strong>which builds trust, and loyalty</strong>. The question may as well ask "Do you trust me?". Microsoft are too scared to ask such a question - they would rather you didn't even think about this question - just focus on the goodies that come in each new release.</p>
<p dir="auto">Can we blame them? Well we can stop using their product. Thing is <code class="notranslate">dotnet core</code> is absolutely fantastic and this isn't a sacrifice I am willing to make for the sake of what is actually being collected. It's a trade off. I am forced to accept a seemingly underhanded way of collecting data just because the platform <em>is something I want to use.</em>. Their licence is pretty clear on the topic:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">License<br>
The Microsoft distribution of .NET Core is licensed with the MICROSOFT .NET LIBRARY EULA. This license includes the "DATA" section to enable telemetry (shown below).<br>
.NET NuGet packages use the same license but don't enable telemetry (see Scope).<br>
DATA. The software may collect information about you and your use of the software, and send that to Microsoft. Microsoft may use this information to improve our products and services. You can learn more about data collection and use in the help documentation and the privacy statement at <a href="http://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=528096" rel="nofollow">http://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=528096</a>. Your use of the software operates as your consent to these practices.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Given that the installer records telemetry on install though - it's arguable whether you can "use the software" (and thus consent to telemetry) before it's actually installed. So sending telemetry on install seems a bit shady - depending on whether that classes as actually having used the software yet.. I imagine that "use" the software means as soon as you launch the installer, not as soon as you run your first <code class="notranslate">dotnet cli</code> command. In which case, the installer can send whatever telemetry home it likes, before you are even aware of it, let alone before you decide to disable it.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">It's very shady and the reason it's shady is because no one gives a crap if they get their data, thus proving again that the customer, even if paying like my good self, comes second.</p>
<p dir="auto">The problem is not that there should be a check box in the installer. It is that the default assumption should benefit the user before the vendor, particularly as this is supposed to be a <em>good citizen</em> open source project. In this case, the telemetry should default to OFF to protect the user's privacy. It should ask to enable it. This applies particularly to the scenarios where it isn't deployed on top of windows and is instead deployed from package repositories on Linux distributions. If you look at the common ecosystems around Debian for example you will not find telemetry enabled by default anywhere. In fact you will see a very strong pro-privacy stance.</p>
<p dir="auto">Personally, I really don't care if the data benefits Microsoft. It's whether or not the collection benefits me and it does not. There are far better ways to engage the customer and take feedback. Like not letting things sit on MS connect for 5 years unfixed, being able to coordinate between the dotnet and clickonce team on critical issues that crippled us for years, actively listening to customer requests on privacy rather than deafening silence while at the same time trying to drown everyone in blogs, marketing etc. Or perhaps fix some well recorded bugs where the start menu stops responding to the keyboard in Windows 10 that has been floating around for 2 years. None of these things get fixed with data; only customer engagement and not the lip service of blog posts, uservoice and other ridiculous abstractions to try and hide the incompetence.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is merely a growing abusive relationship with a rather regressive, data-obsessed corporate America and I'm out. There are better options on the table.</p>
<p dir="auto">If you want an illustration of how much data is being collected, install Fiddler on your PC and let it run for a couple of hours. I personally, and many of us, don't want this to be a de facto standard for software going forwards.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"><div </blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Build (<code class="notranslate">publish</code> command) a <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments-scd" rel="nofollow">standalone/self-contained app</a> (which the <code class="notranslate">dotnet</code> cli allows you to do) with your dev or build server, then you don't even need the dotnet cli installed on you production machines and there is no telemetry to opt out of</p>
<p dir="auto">From <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments-scd" rel="nofollow">Self-contained deployments (SCD)</a></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Why deploy a self-contained deployment?</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Deploying a Self-contained deployment has two major advantages:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>You have sole control of the version of .NET Core that is deployed with your app. .NET Core can be serviced only by you.</li>
<li>You can be assured that the target system can run your .NET Core app, since you're providing the version of .NET Core that it will run on.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">It also has a number of disadvantages:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Because .NET Core is included in your deployment package, you must select the target platforms for which you build deployment packages in advance.</li>
<li>The size of your deployment package is relatively large, since you have to include .NET Core as well as your app and its third-party dependencies.</li>
<li>Deploying numerous self-contained .NET Core apps to a system can consume significant amounts of disk space, since each app duplicates .NET Core files.</li>
</ul>
</blockquote></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"><div class="ReactionPopoverAnchor__B84pko"><button data-component="Button" type="button" class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">Telemetry issue is becoming really very serious once you get with your project into any kind of protected data. Just receiving IP of machines on which CLI is running violates privacy rules as IP is regarded in most EU countries as personal data - it may allow identification of an individual. Obviously one may <strong>turn it off after install</strong> but since it is set to on during install by default it violates active opt in rules.</p>
<p dir="auto">During installation information on CLI telemetry is presented to users but it is not enough according to European Union regulations. If someone wants to collect any sort of data which is not related to basic functionality of provided software it is required by law to present to user active opt in choice with default setting during user interaction being opt-out. So no action from user always means "no telemetry allowed". This endorses rule of <strong>conscious user consent</strong> made after presenting unequivocal choice with default choice being no consent from user.</p>
<p dir="auto">Microsoft entirely unnecessary exposes itself to legal risks at least in all EU jurisdictions ... fact that nothing happened in this area so far is no guarantee that it will not happen in future. Just learn from Facebook problems ....</p>
<p dir="auto">Please take it as a very friendly comment ... like many others in this thread I have invested years in MSFT technologies and would like to see them succeed.</p></div></div><div class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">Maybe what MS should do is build a telemetry manager that all of their tools plug into. Then users would have a central place to opt-in or out of telemetry collection for an entire system.</p>
<p dir="auto">The people complaining about this are probably the same people complaining about telemetry collection in every product that performs that function. If you centralize it, provide a way for people to inspect what is being sent back, and give it a big "OFF" switch, you could turn this whole story around.</p>
<p dir="auto">It would probably also be a good idea to have a telemetry manager to control and protect the server end points that are taking data. Right now every team at MS is rolling their own system for collecting the data. Someone will end up getting that wrong and there will be a data breach. Formalizing your approach to collecting data on the "client" and sending to back end systems for reporting will protect MS as well as other entities.</p>
<p dir="auto">How do you do that on Linux? That's really touchy. You could work with the distro vendors, and start an OSS project for the telemetry manager component. In the end, you are probably only going to be able to collect telemetry if you are VERY explicit about it during install on Linux systems. The overlap of privacy maximalists and Linux users is much higher than with Windows.</p>
<p dir="auto">It's just going to keep coming up, and the "we told you so" moment is coming. You only have to get it wrong once.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"><div class="ReactionPopoverAnchor__B84pko"><button data-component="Button" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">My understanding, from reading the source, of what is happening</p>
<p dir="auto">The runtime itself does not send telemetry so you shouldn't be sending any in telemetry production regardless of the environment setting by using the runtime package and running your pre-built app with the shared runtime by doing:</p>
<p dir="auto"><code class="notranslate">dotnet my.dll</code></p>
<p dir="auto">This is also confirmed as the <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/telemetry" rel="nofollow">intention from the documentation</a></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Telemetry isn't enabled when using the dotnet command itself, with no command attached:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>dotnet</li>
<li>dotnet [path-to-app]</li>
</ul>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Equally a <code class="notranslate">self-contained deployment</code> will produce an executable file that requires nothing to be installed on the target machine and will not send any telemetry when running that executable.</p>
<p dir="auto">The sdk <em>does</em> send telemetry; this is also confirmed as the <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/telemetry" rel="nofollow">intention from the documentation</a></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Telemetry is enabled when using the .NET Core CLI commands, such as:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>dotnet build</li>
<li>dotnet pack</li>
<li>dotnet restore</li>
<li>dotnet run</li>
</ul>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The first install/run at command line  that prints the message about <code class="notranslate">DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT</code> uses the <code class="notranslate">FirstTimeUseNoticeSentinel</code> which does <em><strong>not</strong></em> send any telemetry if it <em>also</em> is printing the message; so you are warned prior to it sending telemetry.</p>
<p dir="auto">It does not send any telemetry after that if the <code class="notranslate">DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT</code> set to one of <code class="notranslate">true</code>, <code class="notranslate">1</code>, <code class="notranslate">yes</code> (case insensitive)</p>
<p dir="auto">The HIPAA example <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/sushihangover/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/sushihangover">@sushihangover</a> gave compiles programs in production so it is using the full <em>sdk</em> rather than just the <em>runtime</em>.</p>
<p dir="auto">The workarounds to the telemetry when using the sdk (<code class="notranslate">build</code>/<code class="notranslate">run</code> etc) as I understand them are:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>either, set <code class="notranslate">DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT</code> environment variable</li>
<li>or, use <code class="notranslate">MsBuild</code> rather than <code class="notranslate">dotnet</code> to build your app - its what <code class="notranslate">dotnet</code> ends up calling and it doesn't send telemetry - its also less convenient; but what you'd probably be using on your build server</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Not sure what the Windows desktop installer does first time; there is a <code class="notranslate">IsDotnetBeingInvokedFromNativeInstaller</code> path which does something different</p>

<p dir="auto">If you receive the message</p>

future. You don't need the Oracle installer. It's mature, cross platform, has a wealth of mature libraries, tools and integrations and the build and deployment infrastructure is done and dusted.  You don't have to use Java if you don't want to either. It was the birth place of a lot of the design methodologies and bits of infrastructure that are crudely copied on the CLR.</p>
<p dir="auto">I'm really wishing I took the blue pill back in 2002 and went down the Java route at this point. The red pill was a bad choice.</p>
<p dir="auto">To be clear, a lot of people are looking at HIPAA compliance as "for use in medical devices". This isn't the case. PII and control of data is the problem. Telemetry is fundamentally incompatible with that as it decreases the signal-to-noise ratio.</p>
<p dir="auto">Another analogy: You don't design a secure system with the starting point of a sieve and try and fill all the holes with environment variables. You start with something that is locked down and open what you need. The problem is that telemetry uses the same protocols and ports as the legitimate and controlled data which adds noise and risk because every communication needs to be understood. That control has to happen in every part of the environment from the workstations the developers use, through to the build infrastructure, through to the production environment. And that is why Windows 10 and this sudden increase in telemetry in developer tooling is an absolute nightmare for us.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">Unrelated to my project research, but another thing occurred to me.</p>
<p dir="auto">In the UK (where I live) we are changing to an opt-out model for organ donation. The rationale is that most people think that organ donation is a positive thing and are not opposed to it, but never get around to opting-in for it. By making it opt-out, the (estimated) minority who—for whatever reason—want to hold on to their organs after they die are able to make that choice, but most people won't do that and many lives will be saved as a result.</p>
<p dir="auto">It's something that is being done for the good of the many, but still provides an opt-out mechanism for the few who are opposed to participating.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" If you did the same analysis by looking at how many people posted on the original github issue for the telemetry feature in the first place, you will find that - most people <em>just don't care.</em> about telemetry full stop. If you were biased you would say that most people don't want any kind of telemetry at all. But I am not biased! (Although my intuition is that this would be closer to the truth)</p>
<p dir="auto">So knowing that, <em>most people</em> don't care about telemetry at all - you can't count these people to lend weight to one side <em>or the other</em> - they are simply compliant with whatever path is carved out for them. This leaves you with only the carers! For me, it should be alarming for microsoft that there are so many people chiming in on this issue. Personally my own concerns would be placated with a simple checkbox on the dotnet cli installer. But I am not going to give up on the platform over this issue - I am not one of the unlucky developers who are purportedly losing contracts over this!</p></div></div><div role="toolbar"
